podcast.body: Recognized as one of the greatest and angriest rock songs of the 1990s from their debut album. Due to its lyrical content, specifically containing 17 instances of the "F-Bomb," the Canadian Broadcast Standards Council's regulations often necessitate radio stations to play a sanitized or truncated version of the song. "Rage with the truncated version of one of the greatest and angriest rock songs of the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: "Killing in the Name" was generated by the Rodney King episode and the LA Riots of 1992 and remains one of the great angry rock and roll protest songs of all time. Rage Against the Machine released four albums between 1992 and 2000 covering many volatile topics — political disillusionment, institutional distrust, the growing gap between rich and poor, police brutality, and oppression of America's black population. "Rage kept everybody honest with four albums between 1992 and 2000, covering many volatile topics."

podcast.body: This song is referenced as a comparison point for the explicit language in The Fugs' "C.I.A. Man," suggesting that The Fugs' early use of profanity was almost as impactful for its time. "It's not quite up there with rage against the machines killing in the name, but it's close."

podcast.body: This song was performed early in Rage Against the Machine's set at Lollapalooza 1993, one of their first performances on the main stage. The immediate impact of the song on the crowd was immense, leading to a collective loss of mind. It contributed to the band's early perception as a "new, young, angry band" at its peak. "They just walked on and they immediately kicked into killing in the name of. And the crowd just lost its collective mind."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was the subject of a grassroots campaign, initiated by a fan from Essex via a single Facebook page, to make it the UK Christmas singles chart number one in 2009. The campaign aimed to disrupt a trend of TV talent show winners or novelty tracks dominating the spot since Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" in 1991, specifically targeting *The Climb* by X Factor winner Joe McElderry. Rage Against the Machine pledged a free UK show if successful, spurring fans to generate a record-breaking 50,000 more downloads than its rival, marking the first time downloads decided the outcome. The band performed the song with its explicit lyrics on BBC 5 and subsequently held their free concert, donating all royalties to homeless charities. "Killing in the name ended up beating up The Climb by 50,000 downloads, and this was the first time in the history of this weird competition that downloads tip the scales."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
